verdict: The ruling's mechanism is correct and proven in-episode: the coda templates in _otr_provenance.py (_NAMED_CODA_BY_STATUS) said the true title in the same episode where the model invented one, and the LIVE routed seam (the pack's announcer_intro_safe_system, not the module constant) already ordered 'Sentence 1 names tonight's work from the WORK line' and was ignored -- prompt wording is conclusively dead, template rendering is the coda's own proven fix. As radio craft, though, 'The Tempest, Act I Scene 2' as written is a citation, not an opening: the shape only ships if the template renders locators as spoken ordinal words (TTS reads 'Act I' as a hazard), marks the LLM subtitle as the show's own ('an episode we call...') so it cannot impersonate a real chapter title, and keeps the title span entirely out of the model's emitted text -- otherwise the invented title simply returns one sentence later, restated in the model's half of the line.
driver_errors: Seam misattribution: the brief quotes 'Do not invent facts' from _ANNOUNCER_INTRO_SYSTEM_SAFE in nodes/_otr_line_composer.py as the instruction that failed, but on public_domain the routed system prompt is the pack seam announcer_intro_safe_system (nodes/story_packs/public_domain/faithful_radio_adaptation.json, routed via _PACK_SEAM_BY_PHASE / resolve_creative_system_prompt in nodes/_otr_creative_prompt_router.py); the module constant is the science-lane fixture. The live seam was STRONGER -- 'Sentence 1 names tonight's work from the WORK line... Use ONLY the WORK title and the proper names in the cast list below; invent none' -- and still failed, which strengthens the driver's conclusion but from the wrong exhibit.

Locator plumbing gap presented as available data: the ruling's public_domain locator is unit_label, but identity_from_meta in nodes/_otr_source_identity.py carries an explicit comment 'unit_label is deliberately NOT read -- see the module docstring'. The data exists at the ledgers as the driver verified, but the shipping identity extractor refuses it by documented design; implementing the ruling means reversing a recorded decision, which the brief never flags.
where_the_shape_breaks: Double-naming: if the model composes prose in the same call that carries the rendered work sentence as context, nothing stops sentence 2 from restating the title in its own words ('...the tale of The Purloined Paper...'). The template guarantees sentence 1; the invention returns one sentence later unless the title span is Python-assembled AFTER the model's contribution and the model is asked to continue, not restate.

TTS pronunciation: 'The Tempest, Act I Scene 2' rendered literally is a TTS hazard -- 'Act I' can be read as 'act eye', and roman numerals vs digits render inconsistently. The locator must be templated as ordinal words: 'Act One, Scene Two'.

public_domain locator is silently empty: any announcer consumer that reads SourceIdentity gets no unit_label (excluded by identity_from_meta in nodes/_otr_source_identity.py), so the locator form never fires on public_domain and every episode falls to the subtitle form without anyone noticing -- the 'Quarter-Deck' example becomes unreachable. Plus the dedupe case the ruling itself names: unit_label == title yields 'The Canterville Ghost, "The Canterville Ghost"'.

Subtitle impersonating a chapter: 'Nonsense Novels: "The Blackwood Enigma"' puts an LLM-invented title in exactly the slot where radio announced real chapters and scenes ('Les Miserables: The Bishop's Candlesticks'), and Leacock's actual chapter titles ('Maddened by Mystery, or The Defective Detective') are stylistically adjacent to the LLM's pastiche titles -- a listener who knows the book hears a chapter they have forgotten. Without an ownership clause the deterministic shape ships a milder version of the same lie: a real work with a fake part-title in the real-part-title position.

media_archive truthiness leak: a shared announcer template that takes SourceIdentity.work_title without gating on source_kind in ADAPTATION_SOURCE_KINDS announces 'a scene from Now See Hear!' -- work_title holds the PUBLICATION on that lane (per the docstring in nodes/_otr_source_identity.py). The brief flags this; the concrete break is any fix placed in a shared composer path without the lane gate.

Rewrite-pass parity: the announcer_intro_rewrite block in nodes/OTR_LedgerScriptWriter.py re-runs the same compose_announcer_intro with work_title threaded from meta. A fix landed at a CALL SITE covers one of the two producers; landed inside compose_announcer_intro it covers both. If the template-rendered sentence lands only in-loop, the rewrite pass restores the invented-title behavior on every rewritten episode.

Author dropped from the opening: the ruling's examples never name the author. 'Nonsense Novels' alone means nothing to a modern listener; 'by Stephen Leacock' is what makes it a real book. Shakespeare survives bare; Leacock does not -- and if the coda ever degrades to the generic sentence (_CODA_BY_STATUS), the episode never names him at all.
recommendations: Q1, radio craft: act/scene as a comma-spliced citation is bibliography read aloud; 1940s practice (Lux Radio Theatre, Mercury Theatre, Favorite Story) named work and author warmly up front and used 'Act One' only as a structural marker, never 'Act I, Scene 2' as a citation string. Example lines under the ruling -- Nonsense Novels: 'Good evening. Tonight, SIGNAL LOST presents a scene from Nonsense Novels, by Stephen Leacock -- an episode we call The Blackwood Enigma. An office in disarray, a detective at his desk, and a mystery that maddens all who touch it.' Moby-Dick: 'Tonight, a scene from Moby-Dick, by Herman Melville -- The Quarter-Deck. The evening watch, a gold doubloon nailed to the mast, and Captain Ahab with something to say.' Shakespeare: 'Tonight, The Tempest, the second scene of the first act -- a sorcerer's island, and a storm that was no storm at all.' Note 'The Quarter-Deck' is Melville's own chapter title and already sounds like radio; act/scene is the only locator format that fights the voice and needs ordinal-word rendering.

Q2, when the subtitle misleads: (a) when it sounds like a real part of the work -- the colon slot is where genuine chapters lived, so the invented title borrows the locator form's credibility; (b) when its register contradicts a fidelity lane ('The Tempest: A Hot Take' promises an angle a faithful adaptation does not deliver); (c) when a real locator exists but dedupe/fallback picks the subtitle, trading a true pointer for a fiction-scented one. The one-clause cure: mark ownership -- 'an episode we call The Blackwood Enigma' -- which tells the listener whose title it is and fully defuses (a).

Q3, the new seam ask: the model's job becomes 'continue a sentence you did not write' -- set the scene and raise intrigue around a fixed noun phrase. It fails narratively at the JOIN: doubled framing (template says 'Tonight...', model opens 'Tonight...' again), blind pronouns (sentence 2 wants 'its hero', 'that office' and needs the rendered sentence as immutable in-context material to refer back to), and register whiplash is a non-issue -- announcers shifted from bibliographic to dramatic register at exactly that seam. So: show the model the rendered sentence, instruct 'continue without repeating the work's name', and assemble the final line in Python.

Q4, what the brief got wrong about the listener: it treats the TITLE as the payload when the AUTHOR is equally load-bearing on public_domain; it treats locator-vs-subtitle as a fallback ladder when they do different jobs (locator = provenance, subtitle = tonight's framing -- the coda is the natural home for act/scene, in the bibliographic register it already speaks); it assumes the citation is speakable as written when it is TTS input; and it undersells the misleading-subtitle case as an edge when on this lane it is the mainline, because the LLM's period-pastiche titles are stylistically adjacent to the source's real chapter titles.

Craft option, not a must: on shakespeare, consider carrying work + subtitle in the opening and leaving act/scene to the coda, where 'from The Tempest, Act One, Scene Two' lands naturally beside the existing attribution sentence.
must_fix: The title span must be Python-assembled and never pass through model-emitted text -- and the fix must live inside compose_announcer_intro (nodes/_otr_line_composer.py) so both producers (the in-loop pass and the announcer_intro_rewrite block in nodes/OTR_LedgerScriptWriter.py) inherit it; a call-site fix covers one of two paths.
Locators render in spoken form: ordinal words ('Act One, Scene Two'), never roman numerals or digits -- the consumer is TTS and 'Act I' is a live mispronunciation hazard.

Resolve the unit_label plumbing before the public_domain locator form can exist: identity_from_meta (nodes/_otr_source_identity.py) deliberately excludes unit_label, and the dedupe (unit_label == title, e.g. 'The Canterville Ghost') must land with the threading, or the shape ships title-comma-same-title.

Any announcer consumer of work_title gates on source_kind in ADAPTATION_SOURCE_KINDS (nodes/_otr_source_identity.py), never truthiness -- otherwise media_archive announces 'a scene from Now See Hear!'.
The subtitle form carries an ownership marker in the template ('an episode we call ...') so the LLM title cannot impersonate a real chapter of the named work on a fidelity lane.
